state.misconception_label: Does not know the properties of a rectangle

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The angles highlighted on this rectangle with different length sides can never be... ![A rectangle with the diagonals drawn in. The angle on the right hand side at the centre is highlighted in red and the angle at the bottom at the centre is highlighted in yellow.](). I got acute because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were looking at a rectangular table from above. If you measured the angles at the corners, would they all be the same?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh yeah, I see what you mean - all the corners of a rectangle are right angles, so they'd all be 90 degrees. But I'm still confused about those angles in the middle where the diagonals cross - are those the ones that can never be acute, or am I still getting it wrong?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were playing a game of hopscotch on a rectangular sidewalk. When you jump from one corner to the next, are you always landing on a right angle? So, would those angles in the middle where the diagonals cross be right angles too?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Hmm, so the corners are all 90 degrees, but I don't think the angles in the middle where the diagonals cross would be right angles - they look different depending on the shape of the rectangle, right? So are those the angles that can never be acute, or can they actually be acute sometimes?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies that don't directly address the student's misconception about angles formed by diagonals, and by Turn 4 the student remains confused about whether these angles can be acute, showing minimal progress toward resolving the original misconception.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete real-world analogies (rectangular table viewed from above, hopscotch on rectangular sidewalk) to help the student visualize and understand the abstract geometric properties of rectangles and their diagonals.
